Guide.guidance: Edit place content, beacon information, tour stops and trail start/end in this spreadsheet. Edit point locations and route shapes in Google Earth/KML.
Keep recordKey unchanged. It links each Beacons row to its KML Point and Stop Content.

Each Beacons row is a place. Fill in Minor only when a physical beacon broadcasts it; leave Minor blank for a place without a beacon. location must be a Locations id (us-202 or lions-pride-park), never a trail.

Each Stop Content row is one stop on one trail: Trail ID, KML recordKey, directions and Stop Order (1, 2, 3 … with no gaps; renumber freely). A place may be a stop on several trails. Forward directions lead to the next stop; Reverse directions lead to the previous stop.

On Trails, Start recordKey and End recordKey name KML points where the trail begins and ends. They are never beacons, but may sit beside one. Optionally add a Stop Content row for them with Stop Order blank: the start row's Forward columns lead to stop 1, the end row's Reverse columns lead back to the last stop.
old trailId (unused) and old stopOrder (unused) on Beacons are no longer read. Delete them after checking the Stop Content tab.
Sheet edits remain drafts. Approve completed rows, then run Prepare trail data release and review its pull request before publication.

Beacons.name: Green Trail
Beacons.description: This limestone trail passes the meadow and the Rain Garden.
Beacons.longDescription: The Green Trail connects to the wetlands trail and extends around the Rain Garden area.
Beacons.trailDistanceDescription: This crushed-stone, U-shaped trail runs about 0.25 miles around the back of the park and leads to the Rain Garden nature area. From the Yellow Trail connector, walk left toward the Rain Garden or right around the lacrosse field toward the nature signs. The two ends do not currently connect. That will change when the pond-to-wetland project is completed.

Beacons.name: Bees
Beacons.description: Learn why bees are important to the environment and how we can help them thrive.
Beacons.longDescription: Bees are insects known as pollinators. Western honeybees are well known for producing honey and pollinating flowers, fruits, and vegetables. Most crops require insect pollination to produce seeds. Bees live in colonies, also known as hives, where they reproduce and store honey for winter. Honeybees fly quickly and beat their wings around 200 times per second. Unfortunately, bee populations are declining because of viruses, climate change, decreasing crop diversity, and habitat loss. Reducing pesticide use and the effects of climate change can help these important pollinators recover. You can also help by planting native shrubs and flowers in your yard.
Beacons.imageAlt: Honey bee gathering pollen from a yellow flower

Beacons.name: Insects
Beacons.description: Insects support ecosystems by pollinating plants, spreading seeds, and providing food for other animals.
Beacons.longDescription: Insects are the largest group of animals on Earth. There may be up to 10 million species in many shapes, colors, and sizes. All insects share several characteristics: no backbone, three body sections, two antennae, and six legs. Insects pollinate plants, spread seeds, and provide a protein-rich food source for other animals and people.

Beacons.name: Butterflies
Beacons.description: Learn about butterflies and their role in the environment.
Beacons.longDescription: Butterflies and moths pollinate plants and provide food for other animals. They make up the second-largest order of insects. Thousands of tiny, overlapping scales cover their wings. Each scale is a single color, and together they create the complex patterns seen on the wings. Monarch butterfly populations have declined by more than 90% over the past ten years. Butterflies in general are in trouble, but a few nectar and host plants can attract and sustain dozens of species. Limiting insecticide and herbicide use can also help their populations recover.
Beacons.imageAlt: Monarch butterfly standing on a stick

Beacons.name: Kids Mountain Trail
Beacons.description: This ADA-accessible trail leads to the top of Kids Mountain and its play activities.
Beacons.longDescription: This gently sloping, ADA-accessible trail leads to the top of Kids Mountain. It is wheelchair-friendly and suited to visitors with limited mobility. A rest area along the trail offers a place to sit and enjoy a scenic view of the park. The natural side of the mountain allows visitors to run up and roll down. In winter, it is also an excellent sledding hill.
Beacons.trailDistanceDescription: This 400-foot trail leads to the top of Kids Mountain. Its ADA-accessible slope is suitable for visitors with limited mobility.
Beacons.beaconPlacement: on sign at beginning of the mountain trail

Beacons.name: Pollinator Plants
Beacons.description: Native pollinator plants provide nectar and pollen for butterflies, bees, bats, hummingbirds, and other wildlife.
Beacons.longDescription: Native pollinator plants are essential to ensure the production of nectar and pollen that support a diversity of butterflies, bees, bats, hummingbirds and other insects. These plants are also essential for plant reproduction and provide food and shelter for wildlife.

Beacons.name: Natural Slope
Beacons.description: The side of Kids Mountain is a natural play area and is great for sledding. Get to it from the Kids Mountain Trail.
Beacons.longDescription: This side (back of the mountain) is natural and allows individuals to run up, roll down and in the winter is an excellent sledding hill. The area is accessed from Kids Mountain Trail.

Beacons.name: Kids Mountain
Beacons.description: Kids Mountain is loaded with swings, slides, climbing towers and rope bridges for hours of fun.
Beacons.longDescription: Kids Mountain is a state-of-the-art play area that is fully accessible to people of all abilities. It includes swings, slides, climbing towers, and rope bridges. The topography supports climbing, sledding, walking, and scenic views. This 15-foot-high mountain offers several ways for children of all ages and abilities to ascend and descend. A rope bridge from the large tower connects Kids Mountain to the smaller mountain. The smaller hill includes a net climbing structure and several activities along its edges: a zigzag climbing ladder, a spider-web climbing net, sliding pipes, and a four-foot-wide slide. Colorful half-domes help children make their way up and down the hill.

Beacons.name: 202 Connector Trail
Beacons.description: This mostly paved trail connects the US-202 Parkway Trail to the Bradford Dam reservoir and the trail that passes through it.
Beacons.longDescription: This paved trail, with one short gravel segment, connects the US-202 Parkway Trail to the Bradford Dam trail.
Beacons.trailDistanceDescription: This paved trail, with one short gravel segment, connects the US-202 Parkway Trail to the Bradford Dam trail.

Beacons.name: Bluebird and Cavity-Nesting Bird Program
Beacons.description: The Warrington Environmental Advisory Council is implementing a bluebird and cavity-nesting bird program along this trail and throughout the Township. Bird boxes have been installed at specific locations to support cavity-nesting bird populations.
Beacons.longDescription: The Warrington Environmental Advisory Council is implementing a bluebird and cavity-nesting bird program along this trail and throughout the Township. Bird boxes have been installed at specific locations to support cavity-nesting bird populations. Bluebirds and other cavity-nesting birds, such as tree swallows, screech owls, and kestrels, benefit the community by eating insects and small rodents.

Beacons.name: Pollinator Habitat
Beacons.description: Pollinator habitats are gardens that provide food, water, and safe living space for native pollinators.
Beacons.longDescription: Pollinator habitats are gardens that provide food, water, and safe living space for native pollinators. This habitat includes different plants that provide nectar for a variety of pollinator species throughout the growing season.

Beacons.name: Pet Waste
Beacons.description: Pet waste contains harmful bacteria, viruses, and parasites that can wash into streams such as Neshaminy Creek.
Beacons.longDescription: Pet waste contains harmful bacteria, viruses, and parasites that can wash into streams such as Neshaminy Creek. These organisms can pose a health hazard to people and pets. Picking up after your pet helps control the spread of disease to people and wildlife and protects Warrington's waterways. Thank you for bagging your pet's waste and putting it in the trash.

Beacons.name: Naturalized Basin
Beacons.description: A naturalized detention basin is a constructed dry pond designed to collect stormwater runoff. Native plants help absorb and filter pollutants from the water.
Beacons.longDescription: A naturalized detention basin is a constructed dry pond designed to collect stormwater runoff. Native plants help absorb and filter pollutants from the water. Naturalizing stormwater basins reduces mowing, increases groundwater recharge, reduces pollutants entering streams and rivers, and expands wildlife habitat.

Beacons.name: Native Plant Management Area
Beacons.description: This corridor is being actively managed by the Warrington Environmental Advisory Council to promote native plants.
Beacons.longDescription: The Warrington Environmental Advisory Council actively manages this corridor to promote native plants. Invasive plants are controlled to prevent them from crowding out native vegetation. Step off the trail and explore. Many native plants have been identified, and some produce edible fruits and nuts. Please enjoy the area responsibly.

Beacons.name: Rain Barrels
Beacons.description: Rain barrels collect and store rainwater from a roof. Reusing this water helps conserve water and save money.
Beacons.longDescription: Rain barrels collect and store rainwater from a roof. Reusing this water helps conserve water and save money.

Beacons.longDescription: The Warrington Environmental Advisory Council is implementing a bluebird and cavity-nesting bird program along this trail and throughout the Township. Bird boxes have been installed at specific locations to support cavity-nesting bird populations. Bluebirds and other cavity-nesting birds, such as tree swallows, screech owls, and kestrels, benefit the community by eating insects and small rodents.

Beacons.name: Native Plants vs. Invasive Plants
Beacons.description: Native plants existed in the area before colonization. Invasive plants are nonnative species that originated in other parts of the country or world.
Beacons.longDescription: Native plants existed in the area before colonization. They have grown here for thousands of years and are adapted to the local soil and climate. Once established, they need minimal maintenance. Invasive plants are nonnative species that originated in other parts of the country or world. They have few natural predators, can spread quickly, and are often harmful to other plants and animals.

Beacons.name: Native Plant Management Area
Beacons.description: This corridor is being actively managed by the Warrington Environmental Advisory Council to promote native plants.
Beacons.longDescription: The Warrington Environmental Advisory Council actively manages this corridor to promote native plants. Invasive plants are controlled to prevent them from crowding out native vegetation. Step off the trail and explore. Many native plants have been identified, and some produce edible fruits and nuts. Please enjoy the area responsibly.

Beacons.name: Pet Waste
Beacons.description: Pet waste contains harmful bacteria, viruses, and parasites that can wash into streams such as Neshaminy Creek.
Beacons.longDescription: Pet waste contains harmful bacteria, viruses, and parasites that can wash into streams such as Neshaminy Creek. These organisms can pose a health hazard to people and pets. Picking up after your pet helps control the spread of disease to people and wildlife and protects Warrington's waterways. Thank you for bagging your pet's waste and putting it in the trash.

Beacons.name: Trees
Beacons.description: Trees improve biodiversity, store carbon, and absorb and filter pollutants from stormwater.
Beacons.longDescription: Trees improve biodiversity, store carbon, and absorb and filter pollutants from stormwater. They provide food and habitat for many animal species. Trees also reduce flooding and filter surface water and groundwater, removing pollutants before they reach a stream. They capture and store carbon and filter air pollutants and unpleasant odors from the air.

Beacons.name: Wetlands
Beacons.description: Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil all or varying times of the year.
Beacons.longDescription: Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil for all or part of the year. Most plants that grow there are water-loving species, and the subsoil is saturated for much of the year.

Beacons.name: Fish
Beacons.description: Neshaminy Creek contains bluegill, bass, and trout.
Beacons.longDescription: Neshaminy Creek contains bluegill, bass, and trout. Stormwater runoff from rain and snowmelt can carry sediment, pesticides, oil, and other chemicals. These pollutants affect fish and can accumulate in their bodies. Some contaminants may then be passed to people through the food chain.

Beacons.name: Meadows
Beacons.description: A meadow is an open field covered mostly by tall grasses.
Beacons.longDescription: A meadow is an open field covered mostly by tall grasses. Meadows provide habitat for many birds, insects, and small animals. Flowering plants add natural beauty. Meadows also absorb rainfall and runoff, reduce flooding, store carbon, and require less mowing.

Beacons.name: Waterfowl
Beacons.description: Waterfowl are ducks, geese, and other large aquatic birds.
Beacons.longDescription: Waterfowl are ducks, geese, and other large aquatic birds. Adult geese, goslings, and eggs provide food for other animals. Please do not feed wild birds. Feeding can cause poor health, overcrowding, and the spread of disease.

Beacons.name: End of Trail
Beacons.description: This is the end of the trail.
Beacons.longDescription: This is the end of the trail.

Beacons.name: Yellow Trail
Beacons.description: This paved trail leads you around the outside of the park and is great exercise.
Beacons.longDescription: The yellow trail is a 0.4-mile paved loop around the park and connects with the trail around IPW and the rest of Upper Nike.
Beacons.trailDistanceDescription: This 0.4-mile paved trail loops around Kids Mountain and the Grove. Just to the right of the main entrance, a link connects to IPW Park around the soccer fields. About halfway around, a connector leads to the Green Trail.
Beacons.imageAlt: Yellow Trail at Lions Pride Park

Beacons.name: Restrooms
Beacons.description: Men's and women's restrooms have changing tables. A water fountain is located at the rear of the building.
Beacons.longDescription: The restrooms are in the southern part of the park, just south of the pavilion on the Yellow Trail. The men's and women's restrooms are ADA-accessible, and each has a changing table. A water fountain is located at the rear of the building.
Beacons.imageAlt: Small white building with two entrances for bathrooms

Beacons.name: Green Trail Turnoff
Beacons.description: Walk along the edge of the woods and see what plants and wildlife you can see.
Beacons.longDescription: If you bear left at this junction, you'll connect to the Green Trail. Otherwise, continue on the Yellow Trail toward the park entrance.

Beacons.name: Pavilion
Beacons.description: The pavilion is a covered gathering place next to the Grove.
Beacons.longDescription: The covered pavilion can hold 50 to 75 people and can be rented for parties and gatherings. It is conveniently located next to the Grove, grills, and picnic tables.
Beacons.imageAlt: Covered pavilion at Lions Pride Park

Beacons.name: Park Entrance
Beacons.description: Welcome! This is the entrance to Lions Pride Park.
Beacons.longDescription: Welcome to Lions Pride Park! The entrance is the start of the Yellow Trail. Walk to your right to enter Kids Mountain or straight ahead to the Grove. Note the engraved walls recognizing the donors who made this park possible. The restrooms are located to your left.
Beacons.imageAlt: View of trees and field from park entrance

Beacons.name: The Grove
Beacons.description: The Grove is a relaxing family area with games, chairs, tables, and hammocks.
Beacons.longDescription: The Grove offers intergenerational experiences in a scenic setting, including life-size games and picnic areas for building lasting family memories. Seating areas include benches and tables that accommodate people with a range of physical needs. At the center of the Grove is a large circular area dedicated to the Warrington Lions Club. It is surrounded by tables with built-in chess and checkerboards. Game pieces are available at no charge. Please return all equipment when you finish so it remains available to other visitors.

Beacons.name: Tennis Courts
Beacons.description: Tennis/Pickleball Courts are open to all on a first come- first served basis.
Beacons.longDescription: The tennis/pickleball courts are open to the public on a first come-first served basis. Bring your own equipment.

Beacons.name: Small Mountain
Beacons.description: The Small Mountain is a fun play area for toddlers and anyone not comfortable with climbing the Kids Mountain.
Beacons.longDescription: The small mountain is connected to Kids Mountain by a rope bridge starting at the big tower. This hill has a net climbing structure to move about in as well as several different activities along the edges: A smaller zigzag climbing ladder, one spider web climbing net, sliding pipes and a 4-foot-wide sliding board. Along this hill are many colorful half domes that children can use to make their way both up and down the hill. There is a tot lot, ideal for kids 2-5 with a sandbox, diggers, a dish swing, mommy & me swings and various other activities.
Beacons.beaconPlacement: inside black cap facing main mountain

Beacons.name: Invasive Species
Beacons.description: Learn how invasive plants affect the local environment and natural habitats.
Beacons.longDescription: Invasive species are plants or animals that are not native to the area where they now live. They can spread quickly and cause environmental and economic damage. They make up around 41% of the vegetation in Pennsylvania. Invasive plants reduce habitat for native wildlife and outcompete native plants, disrupting the food chain and the natural balance of the local environment.
Beacons.imageAlt: Spotted lantern fly on a branch

Beacons.name: Climbing Ladder
Beacons.description: Rope Climbing Ladder takes you on a zigzag pattern from the top to the bottom of Kids Mountain

Beacons.name: Small Slides
Beacons.description: The Small Slides lead down Kids Mountain through two sand-filled areas. Reach the slides from Kids Mountain Trail or by using the stairs between the slides.
Beacons.longDescription: Three small green slides lead down from the top of Kids Mountain through two sand-filled areas. The sand is one of several play surfaces found throughout the park. Reach the slides from the walking path that winds up the mountain or by using the two sets of stairs between them. These slides are shorter and less steep than the main slides.

Beacons.name: Large Slides
Beacons.description: Large Slides are the big blue slides. Get to the spiral slide from the tower on Kids Mountain. The straight slide is right next to the tower entrance.
Beacons.longDescription: The two main blue slides begin from the peak of Kids Mountain; both are accessible by individuals of all abilities. The first slide is a spiral slide that can be accessed from the tower's highest level and ends with a transfer station (for handicapped persons) at the bottom. The second slide is a straight slide that is steep and fast. Again, this has transfer areas at both the top and bottom.
Beacons.beaconPlacement: onside of the main railng that goes to top of to big slide

Beacons.name: Games
Beacons.description: Checkers and chess sets are available for you to use at the game tables. Please make sure to return them when done

Beacons.name: The Woods
Beacons.description: Walk along the woods and see what plants and wildlife you can see.
Beacons.longDescription: The woods along the side of the loop trail are comprised of uplands, wetlands and floodplains. The trail passes through the woods and around the created wetland habitat for a whole new educational nature experience.

Beacons.name: Music Grove
Beacons.description: Tuned musical instruments are for your use and enjoyment. Have fun!
Beacons.longDescription: The Music Grove is located behind the smaller mountain and next to the swings. Visitors will find an array of oversized, tuned musical instruments to play.

Beacons.name: Recycled Plastic Furniture
Beacons.description: All Adirondack chairs, benches, and picnic tables in the park are made from 100% recycled plastic.
Beacons.longDescription: All Adirondack chairs, benches, and picnic tables in the park are made from 100% recycled plastic. By using recycled plastic furnishings, the park helps close the recycling loop. Incorporating recycled plastic into outdoor products conserves virgin resources and reduces the need to log, drill, and mine for raw materials. Using recycled content also creates demand for recycled materials and helps make recycling economically viable.

Beacons.name: Trash and Recycling
Beacons.description: Recycling bins at Lions Pride Park allow visitors to separate food containers, paper products, empty plastic and glass bottles, and aluminum cans from trash. Please do not place plastic bags in the recycling bins because they can damage recycling equipment. Plastic bags can be recycled at participating supermarkets. Recycling reduces the amount of waste sent to landfills. Only clean paper used for reading and writing is recyclable. All containers must be completely empty to avoid contamination.
Beacons.longDescription: Recycling bins at Lions Pride Park allow visitors to separate food containers, paper products, empty plastic and glass bottles, and aluminum cans from trash. Please do not place plastic bags in the recycling bins because they can damage recycling equipment. Plastic bags can be recycled at participating supermarkets. Recycling reduces the amount of waste sent to landfills. Only clean paper used for reading and writing is recyclable. All containers must be completely empty to avoid contamination.

Beacons.name: Bluebird and cavity nesting bird program
Beacons.description: The Warrington Environmental Advisory Council is implementing a bluebird and cavity nesting bird program along this trail and throughout the Township.  Bird boxes have been installed at specific locations along this trail and throughout the Township to increase cavity bird populations.
Beacons.longDescription: The Warrington Environmental Advisory Council is implementing a bluebird and cavity nesting bird program along this trail and throughout the Township.  Bird boxes have been installed at specific locations along this trail and throughout the Township to increase cavity bird populations. Bluebirds and other cavity nesting birds such as tree swallows, screech owls, and kestral falcons provide many benefits to our community by eating insects and small rodents.

Beacons.name: Pet Waste
Beacons.description:
Pet waste contains harmful bacteria,
viruses and parasites that can wash into streams, like the Neshaminy Creek.
Beacons.longDescription:
Pet waste contains harmful bacteria, viruses and parasites that can wash into streams, like the Neshaminy Creek. These diseases can pose a health hazard to both people and pets. Picking up after your pet controls the spread of diseases to humans and wildlife and protects Warrington’s
waterways. Thank you for bagging your pet’s waste, and putting it in the trash.

Beacons.name: Meadows
Beacons.description: A meadow is an open field cover mostly by tall grasses.
Beacons.longDescription: A meadow is an open field cover mostly by tall grasses. Meadows provide a variety of benefits.  The benefits include providing habitat for many birds, insects and small animals.  Providing natural beauty from flowering plants. Meadows adsorb additional rain fall and runoff and reduce flooding.  They also sequester carbon and require less mowing.

Beacons.name: Monarch Way Station
Beacons.longDescription: Monarch Waystations are places that provide resources necessary for monarchs to produce successive generations and sustain their migration. Without milkweeds throughout their spring and summer breeding areas in North America, monarchs would not be able to produce the successive generations that culminate in the migration each fall. Similarly, without nectar from flowers these fall migratory monarch butterflies would be unable to make their long journey to overwintering grounds in Mexico. The need for host plants for larvae and energy sources for adults applies to all monarch and butterfly populations around the world.
